stories.title: Voyager 1 resumes contact after a 48-hour communications pause
paragraphs: JPL said NASA's Deep Space Network lost Voyager 1's signal on Oct. 18–19, 2026, then regained it on Oct. 20 after about 48 hours, before troubleshooting commands could arrive. Space.com notes the probe is nearly one light-day from Earth and will hit that distance on Nov. 18.

Engineers found one thruster group went offline and backups engaged automatically under fault protection. Mission manager Kareem Badaruddin called it the first time the spacecraft has behaved this way. The root cause remains under investigation.

In early September, JPL finished Voyager 1's "Big Bang" power swap—replacing three devices with lower-power alternatives—after a similar change on Voyager 2 about six weeks earlier, aiming to keep remaining science instruments running longer as each craft loses about 4 watts of power per year.

stories.title: Underwater volcano generator briefly makes net-positive electricity off Oregon
paragraphs: ScienceAlert reports that Seattle-based Endurance Energy ran its Adélie seafloor generator at Axial Seamount, about 480 kilometers (300 miles) off Oregon and roughly 1,500 meters (5,000 feet) deep, and said the system produced more electricity than it consumed for 8.7 seconds during a Sept. 27 test announced Oct. 19.

According to ScienceAlert's summary of the company release, hot vent water near 281°C (538°F) drove a turbine to about 26,000 revolutions per minute. After subtracting pump and other loads, Endurance reported a median surplus of about 2 kilowatts during that interval, with a peak of 16.5 kilowatts. The run stopped when a battery safety system tripped; a pump power cable later failed on restart.

ScienceAlert notes the measurements come from Endurance with no peer-reviewed paper yet, and that energy used for shipping, drilling, and installation is not included. CEO Andrew Redd said the next 100-kilowatt Gentoo unit targets longer runs this winter, with first commercial power aimed at Tonga in 2027.

stories.title: Blind listeners and musicians show less internal noise in pitch hearing
paragraphs: In The Conversation, Georgia Tech psychologist Woon Ju Park summarizes a Journal of Neuroscience study comparing nine people blind before age 2 with 18 sighted participants who had varied musical training on tone-in-noise detection and pitch discrimination tasks.

Park writes that early-blind participants outperformed sighted peers only on pitch discrimination, pointing to brain-level processing rather than cochlear frequency selectivity. A mathematical model attributed the advantage to lower internal noise—more consistent responses to the same sound over time.

The same analysis found that musical training similarly reduced internal noise in sighted musicians compared with people who were neither early-blind nor extensively trained. Park says how much training is needed, and whether gains extend to everyday complex listening, remains open.

stories.title: Lyman-alpha radiation may clear fog around early bright galaxies
paragraphs: Universe Today reports that Flatiron Institute researcher Shyam H. Menon and University of Texas at Dallas physicist Aaron Smith argue in The Astrophysical Journal that Lyman-alpha radiation pressure can help explain why JWST sees unexpectedly bright, dense star clusters only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

According to Universe Today, the team post-processed radiation-hydrodynamic simulation snapshots with Smith's COLT Monte Carlo code rather than simulating Lyα self-consistently from scratch. They conclude Lyα is unlikely to stop dense filament star formation, but once star formation saturates it can eject volume-filling gas and dust.

Menon told Universe Today that clearing that diffuse "fog" lets observers see early stars more clearly and can launch fast winds. The paper is titled "Lyα Radiation Pressure in Dense Star Clusters: Implications for Star Formation and Winds at Cosmic Dawn."
